claim: Tissue homeostasis relies on the fine regulation between stem and progenitor cell maintenance and lineage commitment.
source: Tissue homeostasis relies on the fine regulation between stem and progenitor cell maintenance and lineage commitment.
evidence: This is a general statement about tissue homeostasis that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: In the adult prostate, stem cells have been identified in both basal and luminal cell compartments.
source: In the adult prostate, stem cells have been identified in both basal and luminal cell compartments.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Basal stem/progenitor cell homeostasis is still poorly understood.
source: However, basal stem/progenitor cell homeostasis is still poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance is regulated by a balance between BMP5 self-renewal signal and GATA3 dampening activity.
source: We show that basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance is regulated by a balance between BMP5 self-renewal signal and GATA3 dampening activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deleting Gata3 enhances adult prostate stem/progenitor cells self-renewal capacity in both organoid and allograft assays.
source: Deleting Gata3 enhances adult prostate stem/progenitor cells self-renewal capacity in both organoid and allograft assays.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from organoid and allograft assays shown in the figures.

claim: The enhanced self-renewal phenotype of Gata3-deficient cells results from a local increase in BMP5 activity in basal cells.
source: This phenotype results from a local increase in BMP5 activity in basal cells as shown by the impaired self-renewal capacity of Bmp5-deficient stem/progenitor cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing impaired self-renewal in Bmp5-deficient cells.

claim: Bmp5-deficient stem/progenitor cells have impaired self-renewal capacity.
source: This phenotype results from a local increase in BMP5 activity in basal cells as shown by the impaired self-renewal capacity of Bmp5-deficient stem/progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Bmp5 gene inactivation is sufficient to delay prostate cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
source: Strikingly, Bmp5 gene inactivation or BMP signaling inhibition with a small molecule inhibitor are also sufficient to delay prostate and skin cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from mouse models.

claim: BMP signaling inhibition with a small molecule inhibitor is sufficient to delay prostate cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
source: Strikingly, Bmp5 gene inactivation or BMP signaling inhibition with a small molecule inhibitor are also sufficient to delay prostate and skin cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data using K02288 inhibitor.

claim: Bmp5 gene inactivation is sufficient to delay skin cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
source: Strikingly, Bmp5 gene inactivation or BMP signaling inhibition with a small molecule inhibitor are also sufficient to delay prostate and skin cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from mouse models.

claim: BMP signaling inhibition with a small molecule inhibitor is sufficient to delay skin cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
source: Strikingly, Bmp5 gene inactivation or BMP signaling inhibition with a small molecule inhibitor are also sufficient to delay prostate and skin cancer initiation of Pten-deficient mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data using K02288 inhibitor.

claim: BMP5 is a key regulator of basal prostate stem cell homeostasis.
source: Together, these results establish BMP5 as a key regulator of basal prostate stem cell homeostasis and identifies a potential therapeutic approach against Pten-deficient cancers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: BMP signaling inhibition represents a potential therapeutic approach against Pten-deficient cancers.
source: Together, these results establish BMP5 as a key regulator of basal prostate stem cell homeostasis and identifies a potential therapeutic approach against Pten-deficient cancers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing delayed cancer progression with BMP inhibition.

claim: Maintaining homeostasis in adult tissues requires a fine balance between stem cell maintenance and differentiation.
source: Maintaining homeostasis in adult tissues requires a fine balance between stem cell maintenance and differentiation (Morrison and Kimble, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: An amplification of the stem/progenitor cell pool at the expense of cell differentiation is expected to be detrimental to tissue homeostasis.
source: An amplification of the stem/progenitor cell pool at the expense of cell differentiation or, conversely, the depletion of the stem/progenitor cell pool by premature differentiation are both expected to be detrimental to tissue homeostasis (Signer and Morrison, 2013; Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The depletion of the stem/progenitor cell pool by premature differentiation is expected to be detrimental to tissue homeostasis.
source: An amplification of the stem/progenitor cell pool at the expense of cell differentiation or, conversely, the depletion of the stem/progenitor cell pool by premature differentiation are both expected to be detrimental to tissue homeostasis (Signer and Morrison, 2013; Tomasetti and Vogelstein, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dynamic process of stem/progenitor cell maintenance is regulated by signals from the microenvironment (niche) and by intrinsic regulatory mechanisms.
source: The dynamic process of stem/progenitor cell maintenance is regulated by signals from the microenvironment (niche) and by intrinsic regulatory mechanisms (Dumont et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cancer initiation and progression are thought to rely in large part on the self-renewal potential of cancer stem cells.
source: Similarly, cancer initiation and progression are thought to rely in large part on the self-renewal potential of cancer stem cells (Batlle and Clevers, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating stem/progenitor cell homeostasis in the prostate are still poorly understood.
source: In many systems, including the prostate, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating stem/progenitor cell homeostasis are still poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The prostate consists of a multitude of branched epithelial ducts funneling prostatic fluids to the upper urethra.
source: The prostate consists of a multitude of branched epithelial ducts funneling prostatic fluids to the upper urethra.
evidence: This is a description of prostate anatomy based on established knowledge.

claim: Prostatic ducts are composed of an inner layer of secretory luminal cells surrounded by a layer of basal cells interspersed with rare neuroendocrine cells.
source: Prostatic ducts are composed of an inner layer of secretory luminal cells surrounded by a layer of basal cells interspersed with rare neuroendocrine cells.
evidence: This is a description of prostate tissue structure based on established knowledge.

claim: Tissue homeostasis and regeneration of the prostate have been shown to rely on endogenous stem cell populations.
source: Tissue homeostasis and regeneration of the prostate have been shown to rely on endogenous stem cell populations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the following sentence.

claim: Allograft assays and lineage-tracing experiments revealed the presence of stem cells in both the basal and luminal compartments of the prostate.
source: Allograft assays and lineage-tracing experiments revealed the presence of stem cells in both the basal and luminal compartments (Choi et al., 2012; Goldstein et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During homeostasis and regeneration, adult prostate stem cells are largely unipotent.
source: During homeostasis and regeneration, adult stem cells are largely unipotent (Choi et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Basal stem cells act as facultative stem cells by activating basal to luminal lineage conversion under various stress conditions.
source: However, basal stem cells act as facultative stem cells by activating basal to luminal lineage conversion under various stress conditions (Kwon et al., 2014; Toivanen et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Basal stem cells are constitutively multipotent in the developing prostate.
source: In contrast, basal stem cells are constitutively multipotent in the developing prostate, where they populate the luminal cell layer through asymmetric cell divisions (Ousset et al., 2012; Shafer et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the developing prostate, basal stem cells populate the luminal cell layer through asymmetric cell divisions.
source: In contrast, basal stem cells are constitutively multipotent in the developing prostate, where they populate the luminal cell layer through asymmetric cell divisions (Ousset et al., 2012; Shafer et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In prostate cancer, basal and luminal stem cells can both act as tumor-initiating cells.
source: In prostate cancer, basal and luminal stem cells can both act as tumor-initiating cells and are thought to contribute to tumor recurrence (Choi et al., 2012; Goldstein et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Basal and luminal stem cells are thought to contribute to tumor recurrence in prostate cancer.
source: In prostate cancer, basal and luminal stem cells can both act as tumor-initiating cells and are thought to contribute to tumor recurrence (Choi et al., 2012; Goldstein et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: GATA transcription factors have emerged as important regulators of prostate development and cancer.
source: In recent years, GATA transcription factors have emerged as important regulators of prostate development and cancer (Nguyen et al., 2013; Shafer et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During postnatal development, GATA3 is expressed in both basal and luminal cells.
source: During postnatal development, GATA3 is expressed in both basal and luminal cells and plays an important role in lineage specification and tissue organization (Shafer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: GATA3 plays an important role in lineage specification and tissue organization during postnatal prostate development.
source: During postnatal development, GATA3 is expressed in both basal and luminal cells and plays an important role in lineage specification and tissue organization (Shafer et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Nuclear loss of GATA3 is associated with the progression to castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and poor prognosis.
source: In cancer, nuclear loss of GATA3 is associated with the progression to castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) and poor prognosis (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Pten-deficient mouse model of prostate cancer exhibits a progressive loss of Gata3 expression.
source: Accordingly, Pten-deficient mouse model of prostate cancer exhibits a progressive loss of Gata3 expression (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In Pten-deficient mouse model, prostate cancer could be accelerated by an acute loss of Gata3.
source: In this model, prostate cancer could be accelerated by an acute loss of Gata3, or significantly delayed by GATA3 maintenance through transgenic expression (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In Pten-deficient mouse model, prostate cancer could be significantly delayed by GATA3 maintenance through transgenic expression.
source: In this model, prostate cancer could be accelerated by an acute loss of Gata3, or significantly delayed by GATA3 maintenance through transgenic expression (Nguyen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The role of GATA3 in adult prostate stem/progenitor cell homeostasis is currently unknown.
source: Despite this growing body of evidence of the importance of GATA3 in the prostate, its role in adult prostate stem/progenitor cell homeostasis is currently unknown.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The BMP signaling pathway is an established regulator of stem cell homeostasis.
source: Among the established regulators of stem cell homeostasis is the BMP signaling pathway (Oshimori and Fuchs, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BMPs are part of the TGFβ family of signaling molecules.
source: BMPs are part of the TGFβ family of signaling molecules, a group comprised of key regulators of cell differentiation, apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and stem cell homeostasis (David and Massagué, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The TGFβ family of signaling molecules are key regulators of cell differentiation, apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and stem cell homeostasis.
source: BMPs are part of the TGFβ family of signaling molecules, a group comprised of key regulators of cell differentiation, apoptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and stem cell homeostasis (David and Massagué, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BMPs are typically expressed in the stem cell niche.
source: BMPs are typically expressed in the stem cell niche and promote either stem cell quiescence or self-renewal depending on context (Genander et al., 2014; Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004; Tadokoro et al., 2016; Tian and Jiang, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: BMPs promote either stem cell quiescence or self-renewal depending on context.
source: BMPs are typically expressed in the stem cell niche and promote either stem cell quiescence or self-renewal depending on context (Genander et al., 2014; Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004; Tadokoro et al., 2016; Tian and Jiang, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In prostate cancer, BMP6 signaling appears to promote cancer progression.
source: In prostate cancer, BMP6 signaling appears to promote cancer progression (Darby et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2017), while BMP7 induces quiescence in metastatic cancer cells (Kobayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: BMP7 induces quiescence in metastatic prostate cancer cells.
source: In prostate cancer, BMP6 signaling appears to promote cancer progression (Darby et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2017), while BMP7 induces quiescence in metastatic cancer cells (Kobayashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Possible regulation of adult prostate stem cells by BMPs has received little attention.
source: Yet, possible regulation of adult prostate stem cells by BMPs has received little attention so far.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: GATA3 plays a crucial role in the control of basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance.
source: Combining mouse genetics, organoid cultures and RNA-seq analysis, we identify a crucial role for GATA3 in the control of basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance and identify BMP5 as a key effector of this activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: BMP5 is a key effector of GATA3 activity in basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance.
source: Combining mouse genetics, organoid cultures and RNA-seq analysis, we identify a crucial role for GATA3 in the control of basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance and identify BMP5 as a key effector of this activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Targeting the BMP pathway with a small molecule inhibitor significantly slows down cancer progression in the prostate.
source: We further demonstrate that targeting the BMP pathway with a small molecule inhibitor significantly slows down cancer progression in the prostate as well as in the skin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Targeting the BMP pathway with a small molecule inhibitor significantly slows down cancer progression in the skin.
source: We further demonstrate that targeting the BMP pathway with a small molecule inhibitor significantly slows down cancer progression in the prostate as well as in the skin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Gata3 is expressed in both basal and luminal populations of the adult prostate.
source: Taking advantage of a Gata3GFP knock-in reporter mouse strain, we found Gata3-driven GFP expression in both the basal and luminal populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data from a Gata3GFP reporter mouse strain shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Gata3 expression in basal and luminal cells was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis.
source: This finding was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and by immunofluorescence staining of GATA3 in basal and luminal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GATA3 is expressed in basal and luminal cells as confirmed by immunofluorescence staining.
source: This finding was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and by immunofluorescence staining of GATA3 in basal and luminal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Short-term organoids grown from wild type basal cells could be passaged for three to five generations.
source: In this assay, short-term organoids grown from wild type basal cells could be passaged for three to five generations, as the organoids progressively lose their propagation potential (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Wild type organoids progressively lose their propagation potential over passages.
source: In this assay, short-term organoids grown from wild type basal cells could be passaged for three to five generations, as the organoids progressively lose their propagation potential (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Cells obtained from Pbsn-Cre Rosa26G3/G3 mice had a reduced organoid propagation potential.
source: Interestingly, cells obtained from Pbsn-Cre Rosa26G3/G3 mice, which express higher levels of GATA3 upon Cre-mediated deletion of a stop cassette (Nguyen et al., 2013), had a reduced organoid propagation potential (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pbsn-Cre Rosa26G3/G3 mice express higher levels of GATA3 upon Cre-mediated deletion of a stop cassette.
source: Interestingly, cells obtained from Pbsn-Cre Rosa26G3/G3 mice, which express higher levels of GATA3 upon Cre-mediated deletion of a stop cassette (Nguyen et al., 2013), had a reduced organoid propagation potential (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cells derived from Gata3-deficient prostates (Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f) showed an increased organoid-forming potential over several passages.
source: In striking contrast, cells derived from Gata3-deficient prostates (Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f) (Grote et al., 2006) showed an increased organoid-forming potential over several passages (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Organoid size was unaffected by Gata3 expression levels.
source: Organoid size, proliferation and apoptosis levels were unaffected by Gata3 expression levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D-E), indicating that the stem/progenitor maintenance potential rather than cell proliferation or survival is altered in those organoids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Proliferation levels were unaffected by Gata3 expression levels in organoids.
source: Organoid size, proliferation and apoptosis levels were unaffected by Gata3 expression levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D-E), indicating that the stem/progenitor maintenance potential rather than cell proliferation or survival is altered in those organoids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Apoptosis levels were unaffected by Gata3 expression levels in organoids.
source: Organoid size, proliferation and apoptosis levels were unaffected by Gata3 expression levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D-E), indicating that the stem/progenitor maintenance potential rather than cell proliferation or survival is altered in those organoids.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The stem/progenitor maintenance potential rather than cell proliferation or survival is altered in Gata3-deficient organoids.
source: Organoid size, proliferation and apoptosis levels were unaffected by Gata3 expression levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D-E), indicating that the stem/progenitor maintenance potential rather than cell proliferation or survival is altered in those organoids.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing no changes in proliferation or apoptosis.

claim: Testosterone treatment of Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f prostate organoids revealed a decrease in organoids capable of forming lumens.
source: To study the effect of Gata3 loss on cell differentiation, testosterone was added to the media to favor differentiation of Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f prostate organoids which revealed a decrease in organoids capable of forming lumens, pointing to a cell differentiation defect associated with the increase in organoid-forming potential (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F-G.

claim: The decrease in lumen-forming organoids in Gata3-deficient cells points to a cell differentiation defect.
source: To study the effect of Gata3 loss on cell differentiation, testosterone was added to the media to favor differentiation of Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f prostate organoids which revealed a decrease in organoids capable of forming lumens, pointing to a cell differentiation defect associated with the increase in organoid-forming potential (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: In vitro activation of CreERT2 in KRT5+ cells reproduced the increased organoid-forming potential observed with the Pbsn-Cre strain.
source: In vitro activation of CreERT2 in KRT5+ cells reproduced the results obtained with the Pbsn-Cre strain (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Specific inactivation of Gata3 in vitro in luminal cells using Krt8CreERT2 transgene did not lead to an increase in organoid-forming potential.
source: For this, we specifically inactivated Gata3 in vitro in luminal cells using Krt8CreERT2 transgene. This did not lead to an increase in organoid-forming potential (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), indicating that the role of GATA3 in basal stem/progenitor cell homeostasis is restricted to the basal compartment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The role of GATA3 in basal stem/progenitor cell homeostasis is restricted to the basal compartment.
source: For this, we specifically inactivated Gata3 in vitro in luminal cells using Krt8CreERT2 transgene. This did not lead to an increase in organoid-forming potential (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), indicating that the role of GATA3 in basal stem/progenitor cell homeostasis is restricted to the basal compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no effect in luminal cells.

claim: The PRU frequency in the basal population was found to be 1 per 8600 for control.
source: The PRU frequency in the basal population was found to be 1 per 8600 for control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from allograft assays.

claim: Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f gave a PRU frequency of 1 in 3,942.
source: In contrast, Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f gave an average of 1 in 3,942, and Krt5CreERT2Gata3f/f of 1 in 1879 which corresponds respectively to over two- and four-fold increase in steady state stem/progenitor cell numbers in the Gata3-deficient basal cell pool.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from allograft assays.

claim: Krt5CreERT2Gata3f/f gave a PRU frequency of 1 in 1879.
source: In contrast, Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f gave an average of 1 in 3,942, and Krt5CreERT2Gata3f/f of 1 in 1879 which corresponds respectively to over two- and four-fold increase in steady state stem/progenitor cell numbers in the Gata3-deficient basal cell pool.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from allograft assays.

claim: Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f corresponds to over two-fold increase in steady state stem/progenitor cell numbers in the Gata3-deficient basal cell pool.
source: In contrast, Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f gave an average of 1 in 3,942, and Krt5CreERT2Gata3f/f of 1 in 1879 which corresponds respectively to over two- and four-fold increase in steady state stem/progenitor cell numbers in the Gata3-deficient basal cell pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PRU frequency data.

claim: Krt5CreERT2Gata3f/f corresponds to over four-fold increase in steady state stem/progenitor cell numbers in the Gata3-deficient basal cell pool.
source: In contrast, Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f gave an average of 1 in 3,942, and Krt5CreERT2Gata3f/f of 1 in 1879 which corresponds respectively to over two- and four-fold increase in steady state stem/progenitor cell numbers in the Gata3-deficient basal cell pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PRU frequency data.

claim: The difference in PRU frequency between Pbsn-Cre and Krt5CreERT2 likely reflects the deletion efficiency of both transgenic lines in basal cells.
source: The difference between Pbsn-Cre and Krt5CreERT2 likely reflects the deletion efficiency of both transgenic lines in basal cells.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the observed difference.

claim: Histological examination of Gata3-deficient grafts showed ductal structures with multiple alveoli and a lumenized epithelial structure composed of a bilayer of basal and luminal cells.
source: The histological examination of these grafts showed ductal structures with multiple alveoli and a lumenized epithelial structure composed of a bilayer of basal and luminal cells as evidenced by KRT5 and KRT8/18 staining (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: GATA3 is critical for regulating basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance in the prostate.
source: From these results, we conclude that GATA3 is critical for regulating basal stem/progenitor cell maintenance in the prostate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: GATA3 inactivation promotes an increase in self-renewing capacity, leading to a gradual expansion of the stem/progenitor cell pool.
source: GATA3 inactivation promotes an increase in self-renewing capacity, leading to a gradual expansion of the stem/progenitor cell pool.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Cells from passage 0 mostly retained the floxed exon 4 of Gata3.
source: Surprisingly, cells from passage 0 mostly retained the floxed exon 4 of Gata3.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data mapping to the Gata3 locus.

claim: Loss of Gata3 exon four occurred in about 50% of cells at passage 2.
source: However, loss of exon four occurred in about 50% of cells at passage 2, and in the vast majority of cells from passages 3 and 4.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data mapping to the Gata3 locus.

claim: Loss of Gata3 exon four occurred in the vast majority of cells from passages 3 and 4.
source: However, loss of exon four occurred in about 50% of cells at passage 2, and in the vast majority of cells from passages 3 and 4.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data mapping to the Gata3 locus.

claim: The limited efficiency of Pbsn-Cre in basal cells allowed the use of the dynamics of locus deletion as an additional filter to identify GATA3 regulated genes.
source: This finding, likely due to a limited efficiency of Pbsn-Cre in basal cells, allowed us to use the dynamics of locus deletion as an additional filter to identify GATA3 regulated genes.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental strategy based on the observed deletion dynamics.

claim: The comparison of differentially regulated genes between wild type and Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f samples at passages 3 and 4 identified 205 candidate genes.
source: The comparison of differentially regulated genes between wild type and Pbsn-Cre Gata3f/f samples at passages 3 and 4 identified 205 candidate genes (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bmp5 emerged as the candidate with the highest differential expression ratio between wild type and mutant at passages 2, 3 and 4 (up to 48-fold difference).
source: Of interest, Bmp5 emerged as the candidate with the highest differential expression ratio between wild type and mutant at passages 2, 3 and 4 (up to 48-fold difference), while being unaffected at passage 0, when the Gata3 locus is still intact (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bmp5 expression was unaffected at passage 0, when the Gata3 locus is still intact.
source: Of interest, Bmp5 emerged as the candidate with the highest differential expression ratio between wild type and mutant at passages 2, 3 and 4 (up to 48-fold difference), while being unaffected at passage 0, when the Gata3 locus is still intact (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A quantification of Bmp5 levels by qRT-PCR validated the RNA-seq results.
source: A quantification of Bmp5 levels by qRT-PCR validated the RNA-seq results (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The analysis of all differentially expressed genes identified a number of genes regulated by SMAD, BMP, BMPR1a- and BMPR2.
source: In line with the dynamics of Bmp5 expression, the analysis of all differentially expressed genes with the ENRICHR resource (Chen et al., 2013; Kuleshov et al., 2016) identified a number of genes regulated by SMAD, BMP, BMPR1a- and BMPR2 (Software ARCH2 and GEO datasets; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) as well as a strong enrichment for SMAD4 binding sites in the regulatory region of those genes (Software Encode-ChEA; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a strong enrichment for SMAD4 binding sites in the regulatory region of Gata3-regulated genes.
source: In line with the dynamics of Bmp5 expression, the analysis of all differentially expressed genes with the ENRICHR resource (Chen et al., 2013; Kuleshov et al., 2016) identified a number of genes regulated by SMAD, BMP, BMPR1a- and BMPR2 (Software ARCH2 and GEO datasets; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) as well as a strong enrichment for SMAD4 binding sites in the regulatory region of those genes (Software Encode-ChEA; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Canonical BMP signaling has been linked to progenitor cell proliferation and differentiation in the epidermis, hair follicle and intestine.
source: Previous studies have linked canonical BMP signaling to progenitor cell proliferation and differentiation in the epidermis, hair follicle and intestine (Genander et al., 2014; Haramis et al., 2004; He et al., 2004; Lewis et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Relatively little is known about the regulation of stem cell homeostasis by BMPs, notably in the prostate.
source: However, relatively little is known about the regulation of stem cell homeostasis by BMPs, notably in the prostate.

claim: In wild-type prostates, Bmp5 was found to be expressed in all three cell types (basal, luminal, and stromal).
source: In wild-type prostates, Bmp5 was found to be expressed in all three cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).

claim: Gata3 inactivation primarily increased Bmp5 expression in basal cells.
source: Interestingly, Gata3 inactivation primarily increased Bmp5 expression in basal cells, which suggests a specific role for Gata3 in this compartment.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data comparing Bmp5 expression in different cell types.

claim: BMP5 is not a critical regulator of Gata3 expression in the prostate.

claim: BMP signaling is a key mediator of the Gata3-deficient propagation phenotype.

claim: The calculated PRU frequency averaged 1 in 7878 in the wild-type basal population.
